title: Feast food
hookLine: feasts with food: pancakes, fish, cakes
tomorrow: why would anyone walk to the same place every single year?

cards: Some smells are a calendar. Masa steaming in corn husks in December. Pancakes on a Tuesday in February.
Fish on a Friday in Lent. Before anyone says a word, your nose knows what day it is. A feast day tastes like that: like a particular kitchen, on a particular day, with particular people.
And the Bible has a line that asks you to taste first and understand after.

teach.b: It's in the psalms, in the Douay-Rheims: "O taste, and see that the Lord is sweet." Taste comes before see. Then there's a scene in the book of Nehemiah.
The law is read aloud to the people after the exile, and they weep. And they're told: don't be sad.

teach.h: SEND PORTIONS TO THE EMPTY TABLE.
teach.b: Go, eat rich food, drink something sweet, and send portions to those who have nothing ready, because this day is holy.
One to tell a friend: in that scene, the holy day isn't finished until the ones with an empty table get a plate. Catholic kitchens kept that rhythm.
Tradition says Shrove Tuesday pancakes used up the eggs and butter before Lent's fast. Fish on Lent's Fridays is fasting food, the quiet that makes the feast taste better when it comes.
King cake at Epiphany, tamales at Christmas in some families, bread braided for Easter.
And Jesus's first sign in John's Gospel happens at a wedding feast in Cana, where the steward tastes the new wine and tells the groom, "thou hast kept the good wine until now."
A feast in this tradition isn't a break from faith. It's one of the places faith happens, with the mouth.

how: Catholic families often mark feasts with special foods, from pancakes on Shrove Tuesday to king cake at Epiphany and braided bread at Easter, and abstain from meat on the Fridays of Lent.

o: meals Catholics are required to eat by law
the food a priest blesses at the altar
the dishes families make to mark holy days

games.q: which food, which day — tap the pairs.

s: fish on Lent's Fridays is a feast food
it's fasting food: the quiet that makes the feast taste better.
in Nehemiah, the holy day included sending food to people with nothing ready
send portions to those who have nothing ready, because this day is holy.
at Cana, the best wine was served first
the steward says: thou hast kept the good wine until now.

games.q: your family's feast dinner is set for twelve. at Mass that morning you notice a new neighbor who's eating alone this week. what does Nehemiah's holy day suggest?
o: save a plate, or a chair, for the one with nothing ready.
keep the table for family; feasts are for the people who cooked.
skip the big dinner this year so nobody feels left out.
games.why: in Nehemiah, the feast isn't finished until portions go to those with nothing ready. the party stays; the table gets wider.

practice: Take one small thing to eat or drink: a piece of bread, a bit of fruit, a sip of something warm. Smell it first, with your eyes open. Then taste it slowly, the way you would a dish someone spent all day making.
If you pray, you can say, between bites, O taste, and see.

wordCard.voice: Feast food. The dishes that mark holy days: pancakes before Lent, fish on its Fridays, cakes and tamales when the feast comes. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a feast, a holy day kept with joy. the root of feast and festival.

carryVoice: Your line: faith you can taste, with a plate saved for the empty table. Back tomorrow.
